items.stem: Coolidge's claim that taxation can 'destroy' property rights assumes which view of government revenue?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)
options: A. Taxation is legitimate only for 'urgent necessity'
B. All taxation is theft
C. Taxes should fund a welfare state
D. Only tariff revenue is constitutional
items.explanation: Coolidge concedes taxation for 'urgent necessity' but treats anything beyond that as destroying the citizen's right to his own industry — the passage's own limiting principle. The other options go further than, or against, his text.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Coolidge concedes taxation for 'urgent necessity' but treats anything beyond that as destroying the citizen's right to enjoy the rewards of his own industry — the passage's own limiting principle.
option_explanations.B: Coolidge did not say all taxation is theft — he allowed taxation for 'urgent necessity.' 'Theft' goes further than his text.
option_explanations.C: Coolidge did not say taxes should fund a welfare state — his whole argument limits taxation to urgent necessity, the opposite of a welfare state.
option_explanations.D: Coolidge did not argue only tariff revenue is constitutional — his address was about taxation in general, not about restricting revenue to tariffs.

items.stem: Coolidge's confidence that low taxes and limited government produce prosperity was shaken most directly by
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)
options: A. World War II
B. The Cold War
C. The Great Depression
D. The civil rights movement
items.explanation: The Great Depression shattered Coolidge's formula — prosperity did not return when government stayed out, and voters demanded the activist state he had warned against. World War II, the Cold War, and civil rights came later or addressed different questions.

option_explanations.A: World War II did not shake Coolidge's formula — it ended the Depression through massive government spending, but the Depression itself was what discredited his creed.
option_explanations.B: The Cold War came later and addressed foreign policy, not the question of whether limited government produces prosperity.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Great Depression shattered Coolidge's formula — prosperity did not return when government stayed out, and voters demanded the activist state he had warned against.
option_explanations.D: The civil rights movement addressed racial justice, not the economic question of whether low taxes and limited government produce prosperity.

items.stem: Riis's 'slavery' metaphor for the woman's working conditions most directly recalled the rhetoric of
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
options: A. Antebellum labor activists who denounced 'wage slavery'
B. Southern planters defending slavery
C. Confederate generals
D. Abolitionists defending the Fugitive Slave Act
items.explanation: Antebellum labor activists — including the Lowell mill women — called industrial exploitation 'wage slavery,' the exact metaphor Riis reaches for. Planters and Confederates defended slavery; abolitionists never defended the Fugitive Slave Act.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Antebellum labor activists — including the Lowell mill women — called industrial exploitation 'wage slavery,' the exact metaphor Riis reaches for.
option_explanations.B: Southern planters defended slavery — they would never call factory labor 'slavery' as a criticism. Planters used the comparison to claim their slaves were better off.
option_explanations.C: Confederate generals fought for slavery — they did not denounce wage slavery. The metaphor belongs to labor activists, not Confederates.
option_explanations.D: Abolitionists never defended the Fugitive Slave Act — they attacked it. And Riis's metaphor comes from labor rhetoric, not abolitionism.

items.stem: Hamilton's claim that complaining when hurt is 'a right which all free men claim' draws most directly on
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)
options: A. French absolutist theory
B. The traditional liberties of English subjects
C. Spanish colonial law
D. Native American diplomacy
items.explanation: Hamilton appeals to the inherited liberties of English subjects — the common-law tradition that free men may complain of abuses. He invokes no French, Spanish, or Native legal tradition.

option_explanations.A: French absolutist theory supported unlimited royal power — the opposite of Hamilton's claim that free men may complain when hurt.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Hamilton appeals to the inherited liberties of English subjects — the common-law tradition that free men may complain of abuses.
option_explanations.C: Hamilton invoked no Spanish colonial law — his appeal was to English liberties, not Spanish legal tradition.
option_explanations.D: Hamilton invoked no Native American diplomacy — his framework was English common law, not Indigenous tradition.

items.stem: Unlike the Pentagon Papers case, the Zenger trial is most notable for establishing its principle through
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)
options: A. An act of Parliament
B. A presidential pardon
C. A jury's verdict rather than an appellate ruling
D. A constitutional amendment
items.explanation: Zenger won his freedom from a colonial jury that refused to convict — jury nullification established the principle. The Pentagon Papers principle came from the Supreme Court in New York Times v. United States (1971), not from a jury.

option_explanations.A: No act of Parliament established the Zenger principle — the acquittal came from a colonial jury, not from legislation.
option_explanations.B: No presidential pardon was involved — Zenger was acquitted by a jury in 1735, a century before the presidency's pardon power could apply.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Zenger won his freedom from a colonial jury that refused to convict — jury nullification established the principle. The Pentagon Papers principle, by contrast, came from the Supreme Court in New York Times v. United States (1971), not from a jury.
option_explanations.D: No constitutional amendment established the principle — the acquittal was a jury verdict in 1735, decades before the Constitution existed.

items.stem: The jury's acquittal of Zenger demonstrated that colonial juries could
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)
options: A. Levy taxes on the colonists
B. Declare independence from Britain
C. Enforce the Navigation Acts
D. Serve as a check on royal authority
items.explanation: The acquittal showed a colonial jury defying the royal governor's handpicked judges — the jury as a popular check on imperial authority. Juries levied no taxes, declared no independence, and enforced no trade acts.

option_explanations.A: Colonial juries did not levy taxes — taxation was the assembly's and Parliament's business, not the jury's.
option_explanations.B: The jury did not declare independence — that came forty years later. The acquittal was a check on the governor, not a revolution.
option_explanations.C: The jury did not enforce the Navigation Acts — those were enforced by vice-admiralty courts, often against colonial wishes.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The acquittal showed a colonial jury defying the royal governor's handpicked judges — the jury serving as a popular check on imperial authority.

items.stem: Ferraro's emphasis on her immigrant father and working-class roots was intended to
items.stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

In her vice-presidential nomination acceptance address of July 19, 1984, Geraldine Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a woman whose highest goal was a future for her children, telling the nation's oldest political party that the future was within reach. —Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, July 19, 1984 (abridged)
options: A. Present Democrats as the party of working families
B. Appeal to Wall Street donors
C. Defend Reagan's economic record
D. Promote American isolationism
items.explanation: Ferraro's biography — immigrant father, working-class roots — framed the Democratic ticket as the party of ordinary working families against Reagan's Republicans. Wall Street, Reagan's record, and isolationism were the opposite of her message.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Ferraro's biography — immigrant father, working-class roots — framed the Democratic ticket as the party of ordinary working families against Reagan's Republicans.
option_explanations.B: Ferraro did not appeal to Wall Street donors — her biography was working-class, the opposite of a Wall Street pitch.
option_explanations.C: Ferraro did not defend Reagan's economic record — she ran against Reagan. Defending his record would contradict her entire message.
option_explanations.D: Ferraro did not promote isolationism — her message was about working families and Democratic values, not about withdrawing from the world.

items.stem: Ferraro's candidacy faced sustained attacks centered on
items.stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

In her vice-presidential nomination acceptance address of July 19, 1984, Geraldine Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a woman whose highest goal was a future for her children, telling the nation's oldest political party that the future was within reach. —Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, July 19, 1984 (abridged)
options: A. Her support for Prohibition
B. Her Civil War military record
C. Her family's finances and tax disclosures
D. Her opposition to woman suffrage
items.explanation: Questions about her husband John Zaccaro's real-estate dealings and the couple's tax returns dogged Ferraro for weeks in 1984. Prohibition, the Civil War, and suffrage had nothing to do with her campaign.

option_explanations.A: Prohibition was long dead by 1984 — Ferraro's campaign had nothing to do with it.
option_explanations.B: Ferraro had no Civil War military record — she was a 20th-century congresswoman. The question is about her 1984 campaign.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Questions about her husband John Zaccaro's real-estate dealings and the couple's tax returns dogged Ferraro for weeks in 1984.
option_explanations.D: Ferraro did not oppose woman suffrage — she was its beneficiary, the first woman on a major-party national ticket. Opposition to suffrage was the opposite of her position.

items.stem: Ferraro's barrier-breaking role is most directly comparable to
items.stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

In her vice-presidential nomination acceptance address of July 19, 1984, Geraldine Ferraro described herself as the daughter of working Americans and of a woman whose highest goal was a future for her children, telling the nation's oldest political party that the future was within reach. —Paraphrase of Geraldine Ferraro, acceptance address, July 19, 1984 (abridged)
options: A. Abigail Adams's letters
B. Clara Barton's nursing
C. Phyllis Schlafly's activism
D. Shirley Chisholm's 1972 run for the Democratic presidential nomination
items.explanation: Chisholm's 1972 campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination broke the same kind of national-ticket barrier Ferraro broke twelve years later. Adams wrote letters, Barton nursed soldiers, and Schlafly organized against the ERA.

option_explanations.A: Abigail Adams's letters were private correspondence, not a barrier-breaking national candidacy. Her role was different in kind from Ferraro's.
option_explanations.B: Clara Barton's nursing was humanitarian service, not a national political candidacy. Her barrier-breaking was in a different field.
option_explanations.C: Phyllis Schlafly's activism opposed the ERA — she organized against the feminist movement Ferraro represented. Schlafly was the opposition, not the parallel.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Shirley Chisholm's 1972 campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination broke the same kind of national-ticket barrier Ferraro broke twelve years later.

items.stem: McGovern's 1972 presidential candidacy was built most directly on
items.stimulus:
Questions 29–32 refer to the following quotation.

In an April 25, 1967 speech, Senator George McGovern argued that the war had begun as a struggle among Vietnamese groups before American intervention, and charged that the United States seemed determined to save Vietnam from Ho Chi Minh even at the cost of destroying the country. —Paraphrase of George McGovern, "The Lessons of Vietnam," April 25, 1967 (abridged)
options: A. Support for escalating the war
B. The Watergate scandal
C. Opposition to the Vietnam War
D. Opposition to the New Deal
items.explanation: McGovern's 1972 'Come home, America' campaign made opposition to the war his defining cause. He never supported escalation, Watergate broke later, and he was a New Deal liberal, not its opponent.

option_explanations.A: McGovern never supported escalating the war — his 1972 campaign was built on ending it. Escalation was Nixon's policy, not McGovern's.
option_explanations.B: Watergate broke in 1972–73 — McGovern's candidacy was built on Vietnam opposition, which predated the scandal.
option_explanations.C: Correct. McGovern's 1972 'Come home, America' campaign made opposition to the Vietnam War his defining cause.
option_explanations.D: McGovern did not oppose the New Deal — he was a New Deal liberal. His candidacy was built on Vietnam, not on attacking the New Deal.

items.stem: Like Vietnam-era dissent, opposition to the Mexican War was led significantly by
items.stimulus:
Questions 29–32 refer to the following quotation.

In an April 25, 1967 speech, Senator George McGovern argued that the war had begun as a struggle among Vietnamese groups before American intervention, and charged that the United States seemed determined to save Vietnam from Ho Chi Minh even at the cost of destroying the country. —Paraphrase of George McGovern, "The Lessons of Vietnam," April 25, 1967 (abridged)
options: A. A young Illinois congressman — Abraham Lincoln
B. A sitting president
C. A Supreme Court justice
D. A foreign ambassador
items.explanation: Lincoln, as a freshman Illinois congressman, attacked Polk's war with his 'spot resolutions' demanding to know the exact spot of American bloodshed — the direct ancestor of Vietnam-era congressional dissent. No president, justice, or ambassador led the opposition.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Lincoln, as a freshman Illinois congressman, attacked Polk's Mexican War with his 'spot resolutions' demanding to know the exact spot of American bloodshed — the direct ancestor of Vietnam-era congressional dissent.
option_explanations.B: No sitting president led opposition to the Mexican War — Polk was the war's champion. Presidential opposition is the opposite of what happened.
option_explanations.C: No Supreme Court justice led opposition to the Mexican War — the dissent came from Congress, led by figures like Lincoln.
option_explanations.D: No foreign ambassador led the opposition — the dissent was domestic and congressional.

items.stem: Wheatley's direct address to 'Christians' indicates her audience was
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)
options: A. Enslaved Africans planning revolt
B. White Christians, whom she challenged on their own religious terms
C. The British Parliament
D. Native American leaders
items.explanation: Wheatley argues inside Christianity — 'Remember, Christians' — turning her white readers' own faith against racial scorn. She addresses no enslaved rebels, no Parliament, and no Native leaders.

option_explanations.A: Wheatley was not addressing enslaved Africans planning revolt — her 'Remember, Christians' is directed at white readers, on their own religious terms.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Wheatley argues inside Christianity — 'Remember, Christians' — turning her white readers' own faith against racial scorn. She addresses no enslaved rebels, no Parliament, and no Native leaders.
option_explanations.C: Wheatley was not addressing the British Parliament — her poem speaks to Christians generally, challenging white racial scorn on religious grounds.
option_explanations.D: Wheatley was not addressing Native American leaders — her subject is Black spiritual equality before a white Christian audience.

items.stem: Wheatley's insistence on Black spiritual equality most directly anticipated the arguments of
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)
options: A. Southern defenders of slavery
B. Twentieth-century isolationists
C. Nineteenth-century Black abolitionists like Frederick Douglass
D. Loyalist pamphleteers
items.explanation: Wheatley's claim that Black souls share in salvation anticipates Douglass and the Black abolitionists, who made Christian equality the moral core of antislavery. Southern defenders, isolationists, and Loyalists argued the opposite or not at all.

option_explanations.A: Southern defenders of slavery argued the opposite of Wheatley — they used Christianity to justify bondage. Her spiritual-equality argument anticipated their opponents.
option_explanations.B: Twentieth-century isolationists argued about foreign policy, not Black spiritual equality. The connection is nonexistent.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Wheatley's claim that Black souls share in salvation anticipates Frederick Douglass and the Black abolitionists, who made Christian equality the moral core of antislavery.
option_explanations.D: Loyalist pamphleteers argued for obedience to Britain, not for Black spiritual equality. Their cause was different entirely.

items.stem: Wheatley's 1773 publication was remarkable because
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)
options: A. Poetry was illegal in the colonies
B. Women could not own property
C. Boston had no printing presses
D. Enslaved people were systematically denied literacy and a public voice
items.explanation: Colonial law and custom barred enslaved people from literacy and public voice — which is why an enslaved woman's published book electrified the Atlantic world. Poetry was legal, Boston had presses, and property is beside the point.

option_explanations.A: Poetry was not illegal in the colonies — Wheatley's book was remarkable for who wrote it, not for its genre.
option_explanations.B: Women's property rights are beside the point — the barrier Wheatley broke was literacy and a public voice for an enslaved person.
option_explanations.C: Boston had printing presses — her book was printed. The absence of presses was not the obstacle.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Colonial law and custom barred enslaved people from literacy and public voice — which is why an enslaved woman's published book electrified the Atlantic world.

items.stem: Wheatley's use of Christian doctrine to attack racial prejudice most directly parallels
items.stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following quotation.

"Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / 'Their colour is a diabolic die.' / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train." —Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773 (abridged)
options: A. Abolitionists citing Scripture against slavery
B. Slaveholders citing Scripture to defend slavery
C. Deists rejecting revelation
D. Loyalists citing Romans 13 to demand obedience
items.explanation: Like Wheatley, abolitionists wielded Scripture against racial oppression — the Bible as a weapon for equality. Slaveholders also cited Scripture, but to defend bondage; deists and Loyalists used it differently or not at all.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Like Wheatley, abolitionists wielded Scripture against racial oppression — the Bible as a weapon for equality.
option_explanations.B: Slaveholders also cited Scripture, but to defend bondage — the opposite use from Wheatley's attack on racial prejudice.
option_explanations.C: Deists rejected revelation — they did not wield Christian doctrine at all. Wheatley's method was the opposite of deism.
option_explanations.D: Loyalists cited Romans 13 to demand obedience to Britain — a different use of Scripture for a different cause, not an attack on racial prejudice.

items.stem: Beveridge's claim that America does 'but what our fathers did' frames imperialism as
items.stimulus:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following quotation.

"If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did—we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward—we only continue the march of the flag?" —Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898 (abridged)
options: A. A complete break with American tradition
B. The natural continuation of westward expansion
C. A return to isolationism
D. An imitation of French republicanism
items.explanation: Beveridge's whole move is continuity: 'we do but what our fathers did — we only continue the march of the flag.' He sells empire as westward expansion carried overseas, not as a break, a retreat, or a French import.

option_explanations.A: Beveridge argued the opposite of a break — 'we do but what our fathers did.' A complete break with tradition is what his critics claimed; he claimed continuity.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Beveridge's whole move is continuity: 'we do but what our fathers did — we only continue the march of the flag.' He sells empire as westward expansion carried overseas.
option_explanations.C: Beveridge did not advocate isolationism — he was arguing for annexing the Philippines, the opposite of retreat.
option_explanations.D: Beveridge did not invoke French republicanism — his comparisons were to England and Germany governing foreign lands, and his continuity claim was to American fathers, not France.

items.stem: William Penn was a member of which of the following persecuted religious groups?
items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following document.

William Penn's Charter of Privileges, granted to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania and the Territories on October 28, 1701, which guaranteed religious toleration and representative government.
options: (A) Roman Catholics
(B) Puritans
(C) Quakers
(D) Anglicans
items.explanation: Penn was a Quaker, and Pennsylvania was founded as a refuge for Quakers and other dissenters persecuted in England. Catholics founded Maryland; Puritans founded New England.

option_explanations.A: Penn was not a Roman Catholic — Catholics founded Maryland under Lord Baltimore, not Pennsylvania.
option_explanations.B: Penn was not a Puritan — Puritans founded New England. Penn's persecuted group was the Quakers.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Penn was a Quaker, and Pennsylvania was founded as a refuge for Quakers and other dissenters persecuted in England.
option_explanations.D: Penn was not an Anglican — the Anglicans were the established church doing the persecuting. Penn belonged to the persecuted Quakers.

items.stem: Because of Penn's Charter of Privileges, Pennsylvania became known for which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following document.

William Penn's Charter of Privileges, granted to the inhabitants of Pennsylvania and the Territories on October 28, 1701, which guaranteed religious toleration and representative government.
options: (A) Exceptional religious diversity
(B) Strict religious uniformity
(C) Witch trials and popular superstition
(D) Hostility toward all religious practice
items.explanation: The Charter's guarantee of religious toleration drew Quakers, Germans, Scots-Irish, and others, making Pennsylvania the most religiously diverse colony. Witch trials belong to Massachusetts; Penn welcomed faith, not suppressed it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Charter's guarantee of religious toleration drew Quakers, Germans, Scots-Irish, and others, making Pennsylvania the most religiously diverse colony.
option_explanations.B: Pennsylvania did not enforce religious uniformity — the Charter guaranteed toleration. Uniformity was the opposite of Penn's design.
option_explanations.C: Witch trials belong to Massachusetts (Salem, 1692) — Pennsylvania was known for toleration, not witchcraft panics.
option_explanations.D: Pennsylvania was not hostile to religious practice — the Charter welcomed faith. Hostility to religion was the opposite of its reputation.

items.stem: Jefferson's 'Revolution of 1800' reversed Federalist policies by
items.stimulus:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following quotation.

"The man who mounted the steps of the Capitol, March 4, 1801 … Jefferson was very tall, six feet two-and-a-half inches in height; sandy-complexioned; shy in manner, seeming cold; awkward in attitude … this loose, shackling person … belonged to the controlling influences of American history." —Henry Adams, History of the United States During the Administration of Thomas Jefferson, 1889 (abridged)
options: A. Expanding the navy and raising tariffs
B. Creating a new national bank
C. Reducing the army, cutting taxes, and paying down the debt
D. Declaring war on France
items.explanation: The 'Revolution of 1800' was a policy revolution: Jefferson shrank the army and navy, repealed internal taxes, and attacked the national debt. He built no new bank, raised no tariffs, and made no war on France.

option_explanations.A: Jefferson did not expand the navy or raise tariffs — he shrank the military and repealed internal taxes. Expansion was the opposite of his program.
option_explanations.B: Jefferson did not create a new national bank — he opposed the Bank of the United States and let its influence wane. A new bank was never his policy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The 'Revolution of 1800' was a policy revolution: Jefferson shrank the army and navy, repealed internal taxes, and attacked the national debt.
option_explanations.D: Jefferson did not declare war on France — he pursued peace and bought Louisiana from Napoleon. War with France was never his policy.

items.stem: Adams's depiction of Washington as a cultural backwater illustrates
items.stimulus:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following quotation.

"The man who mounted the steps of the Capitol, March 4, 1801 … Jefferson was very tall, six feet two-and-a-half inches in height; sandy-complexioned; shy in manner, seeming cold; awkward in attitude … this loose, shackling person … belonged to the controlling influences of American history." —Henry Adams, History of the United States During the Administration of Thomas Jefferson, 1889 (abridged)
options: A. How new and unformed the national government still was
B. British cultural superiority over America
C. The city's rapid industrialization
D. Southern economic dominance of the nation
items.explanation: Adams's village-capital — politicians 'living like bears' without court or commerce — shows a national government still inventing itself from nothing. It illustrates newness, not British superiority, industry, or Southern dominance.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Adams's village-capital — politicians 'living like bears' without court or commerce — shows a national government still inventing itself from nothing, new and unformed.
option_explanations.B: Adams does not argue British cultural superiority — his point is about the newness of the American government, not about Britain's advantages.
option_explanations.C: Washington was not industrializing — Adams depicts a muddy village, not factories. Industrialization is the opposite of his image.
option_explanations.D: Adams does not depict Southern economic dominance — his subject is the unformed national capital, not sectional economics.

items.stem: Roosevelt addressed the ACLU in March 1940 because
items.stimulus:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following quotation.

In a March 14, 1940 address to the American Civil Liberties Union, Eleanor Roosevelt said that traveling the country had made her conscious of the importance of civil liberties, warned that democracy is endangered whenever the light of liberty grows dim, and argued that while wartime nations lose freedoms of press, speech, and assembly, Americans at peace had a grave responsibility to guard them. —Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt, address to the ACLU, Chicago, March 14, 1940 (abridged)
options: A. She supported the internment of Japanese Americans
B. She feared war would again erode civil liberties as in World War I
C. The ACLU had opposed the New Deal
D. The Cold War had already begun
items.explanation: Roosevelt spoke to the ACLU as Europe went to war because she feared a repeat of 1917–18, when dissent was criminalized — the motive for her warning. She never supported internment, the ACLU backed civil liberties, and the Cold War had not begun.

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt never supported the internment of Japanese Americans — she was one of the administration's internal critics of it. Support was the opposite of her position.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Roosevelt spoke to the ACLU as Europe went to war because she feared a repeat of 1917–18, when dissent was criminalized — the motive for her warning that Americans must guard civil liberties.
option_explanations.C: The ACLU did not oppose the New Deal — it was a civil-liberties organization, and Roosevelt addressed it on liberties, not on New Deal politics.
option_explanations.D: The Cold War had not begun in March 1940 — it started after World War II. Roosevelt's concern was a repeat of World War I's repression.

items.stem: Like Roosevelt in 1940, critics of the Patriot Act argued that
items.stimulus:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following quotation.

In a March 14, 1940 address to the American Civil Liberties Union, Eleanor Roosevelt said that traveling the country had made her conscious of the importance of civil liberties, warned that democracy is endangered whenever the light of liberty grows dim, and argued that while wartime nations lose freedoms of press, speech, and assembly, Americans at peace had a grave responsibility to guard them. —Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt, address to the ACLU, Chicago, March 14, 1940 (abridged)
options: A. Civil liberties are unimportant in wartime
B. Only wartime justifies free speech
C. The ACLU should be abolished
D. National crises tempt governments to trade liberty for security
items.explanation: Both Roosevelt and the Patriot Act's critics make the same argument: fear and crisis tempt even free governments to trade liberty for security. Neither side claims liberties are unimportant or that the ACLU should vanish.

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt and the Patriot Act's critics never claimed civil liberties are unimportant in wartime — they claimed the opposite: liberties must be guarded precisely when crisis tempts their surrender.
option_explanations.B: Neither side claimed only wartime justifies free speech — their argument is that liberty must be defended in peacetime too, against the temptations of crisis.
option_explanations.C: Neither side called for abolishing the ACLU — Roosevelt was addressing the ACLU as an ally, and the Patriot Act's critics invoked the same liberties the ACLU defends.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Both Roosevelt and the Patriot Act's critics make the same argument: fear and crisis tempt even free governments to trade liberty for security.
